quizName: DMV Practice Test #14 20 Questions • Passing Score 16

questions.question: When riding in a group, where should inexperienced riders position themselves?

options.text: Just behind the leader.
In front of the group.
At the rear of the group.
Beside the leader.

questions.correctAnswerText: Just behind the leader.
questions.explanation: Inexperienced riders should ride just behind the leader. This lets experienced riders behind them watch and help if needed.

questions.question: What is the minimum following distance when riding at night?

options.text: Two seconds.
Three seconds.
Four seconds.
Five seconds.

questions.correctAnswerText: Three seconds.
questions.explanation: At night, it is harder to see and judge distances. Keep at least three seconds between you and the vehicle ahead. You may need extra time to see that the vehicle has stopped and to slow down or stop.

questions.question: What should you do when going through a curve?

options.text: Always stay in the same portion of the lane throughout the entire curve.
Always stay in the left portion of the lane throughout the entire curve.
Always stay in the right portion of the lane throughout the entire curve.
Remember that the best path may not follow the curve of the road.

questions.correctAnswerText: Remember that the best path may not follow the curve of the road.
questions.explanation: Conditions change all the time. Be ready to move to a different lane position when needed. The best path through a curve may not match the road's curve.

questions.question: On a slippery surface, which action should you avoid?

options.text: Reduce your speed.
Avoid making sudden moves.
Use only the front brake when slowing or stopping.
Use both brakes when slowing or stopping.

questions.correctAnswerText: Use only the front brake when slowing or stopping.
questions.explanation: On slippery surfaces, use both brakes when slowing or stopping, go slower, and avoid sudden movements. Watch for oil, dirt, gravel, shade, and bridges—these areas are more slippery.

questions.question: If a driver is tailgating you, what should you do?

options.text: Flash your brake light before you slow to warn the other driver.
Accelerate.
Pull over to the side of the road.
Slow down.

questions.correctAnswerText: Flash your brake light before you slow to warn the other driver.
questions.explanation: Flash your brake light before slowing down. The tailgater may not see upcoming hazards that require traffic to slow down.

questions.question: How does a motorcycle's stopping distance compare to a car's stopping distance?

options.text: Cars need much longer to stop.
Cars need a little longer to stop.
Motorcycles need longer to stop.
Both motorcycles and cars take about the same amount of time to stop.

questions.correctAnswerText: Both motorcycles and cars take about the same amount of time to stop.
questions.explanation: Under normal conditions, motorcycles and cars stop in about the same amount of time. However, slippery pavement makes stopping very difficult for motorcycles.

questions.question: How should you cross railroad tracks that run parallel to your lane?

options.text: Edge gradually across the tracks.
Cross the tracks at a 90-degree angle.
Wait for the tracks to end.
Move away from the tracks, turn, and cross at an angle of at least 45 degrees.

questions.correctAnswerText: Move away from the tracks, turn, and cross at an angle of at least 45 degrees.
questions.explanation: To safely cross railroad tracks, trolley tracks, or ruts running parallel to your lane, move to a position that lets you cross at an angle of at least 45 degrees. Make a quick, sharp turn. If you try to edge across slowly, the tracks could catch your tires and throw you off balance.

questions.question: When riding through a turn, how should you look?

options.text: Turn your head and shoulders to look through turns.
Keep your arms straight.
Keep your knees away from the gas tank.
Turn just your head and eyes to look through turns.

questions.correctAnswerText: Turn just your head and eyes to look through turns.
questions.explanation: Look through the turn to where you want to go. Turn only your head, not your shoulders. Keep your eyes level with the horizon.

questions.question: What helps other drivers see you at an intersection?

options.text: Try to make eye contact with other drivers.
Ride with your headlight on.
Reduce your space cushion.
Ride in a weaving pattern.

questions.correctAnswerText: Ride with your headlight on.
questions.explanation: Keep your headlight on at all times and ride in a lane position that makes it easy for oncoming traffic to see you. Maintain space to take action if needed. Never assume a driver sees you, even if you make eye contact.

questions.question: To prevent fatigue on long rides, which action should you avoid?

options.text: Dress warmly.
Limit the distance traveled in a day.
Take frequent rest breaks.
Take artificial stimulants.

questions.correctAnswerText: Take artificial stimulants.
questions.explanation: Dress to protect yourself from wind and rain. Ride no more than about six hours per day and take a break at least every two hours. Avoid artificial stimulants because you may feel very tired when they wear off.

questions.question: When another motorcycle passes you from behind, what should you do?

options.text: Move onto the shoulder.
Use the left portion of your lane.
Use the center portion of your lane.
Use the right portion of your lane.

questions.correctAnswerText: Use the center portion of your lane.
questions.explanation: The center portion of your lane is the safest position when being passed. Riding on the side closer to the passing vehicle risks a collision. Riding on the far side may cause the other driver to cut back in front of you too soon.

questions.question: When do you need less space between you and the vehicle ahead?

options.text: When the pavement is slippery.
When you cannot see through the vehicle ahead.
When weather and traffic conditions are perfect.
When traffic is heavy.

questions.correctAnswerText: When weather and traffic conditions are perfect.
questions.explanation: You need more space in bad conditions. Increase your following distance if the pavement is slippery, you cannot see ahead, or traffic is heavy.

questions.question: When following a car, where should you ride in the lane?

options.text: The left portion.
The center portion.
The right portion.
The left or right portions.

questions.correctAnswerText: The center portion.
questions.explanation: Ride in the center of the lane so the driver can see you in their rearview mirror. Drivers check rearview mirrors more often than side mirrors, so this position helps them see you.

questions.question: If you need to swerve to avoid an obstacle, what is important to remember?

options.text: Always brake before swerving.
Do one action, then the other.
Always brake after swerving.
Swerve toward the obstacle.

questions.correctAnswerText: Do one action, then the other.
questions.explanation: Never brake and swerve at the same time. Swerve first and then brake, or brake first and then swerve.

questions.question: What happens if you forget to turn off your turn signal after turning?

options.text: Other drivers may turn into your path.
Others won't see your brake light.
Other drivers will stay away from you and crash risk goes down.
Others will follow you too closely.

questions.correctAnswerText: Other drivers may turn into your path.
questions.explanation: Always turn off your signal after completing a turn. A left-on signal may make drivers think you plan to turn again, causing them to move into your path.

questions.question: In Pennsylvania, what blood alcohol content (BAC) is considered operating under the influence?

options.text: 0.04 percent.
0.08 percent.
0.1 percent.
0.12 percent.

questions.correctAnswerText: 0.08 percent.
questions.explanation: In Pennsylvania, a BAC of 0.08 percent or higher means you are operating under the influence. This is illegal and dangerous.

questions.question: How should you ride over an object on the road?

options.text: Stay seated until you pass it.
Rise slightly off the seat.
Edge over it slowly.
Grip the gas tank tightly with your knees.

questions.correctAnswerText: Rise slightly off the seat.
questions.explanation: Rise slightly off the seat and put your weight on the footrests. This lets your knees and elbows absorb the impact instead of your body, reducing the risk of being thrown from the motorcycle.

questions.question: What is the best way to help others see your motorcycle?

options.text: Always ride in the left portion of the lane.
Wear a white helmet.
Stay in the center portion of the lane.
Ride with your headlight turned on.

questions.correctAnswerText: Ride with your headlight turned on.
questions.explanation: Riding with your headlight on is the most effective way to help others see you, even during the day.

questions.question: How can you reduce the time you need to react to a hazard?

options.text: Always ride under the speed limit.
Keep your hands near the clutch and brakes.
Shift into neutral when slowing down.
Pull the clutch when turning.

questions.correctAnswerText: Keep your hands near the clutch and brakes.
questions.explanation: In high-risk areas like school zones or construction zones, cover the clutch and both brakes. This reduces your reaction time if a hazard appears.

questions.question: Where should inexperienced riders position themselves in a group?

options.text: Just behind the leader.
In the front of the group.
At the back of the group.
Beside the lead rider.

questions.correctAnswerText: Just behind the leader.
questions.explanation: Inexperienced riders should ride just behind the leader. This way they won't fall behind, and experienced riders can watch them from behind.
